entities.summary:
Augustin Daniel Belliard, born in Fontenay-le-Comte, Vendée, in 1769, rose from humble origins to become a prominent French general of the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars, ultimately attaining the title of Comte de l'Empire. His career, spanning from the tumultuous early days of the Revolution to the final defeat of Napoleon, encapsulates the profound social mobility and military dynamism characteristic of this era in Western Europe. Belliard's strategic acumen and unwavering loyalty made him a trusted aide to Napoleon Bonaparte, positioning him at the heart of military operations that reshaped the political map of Europe and beyond, from the Egyptian Campaign to the Peninsular War and the Russian Campaign.

Belliard's military service began with the outbreak of the French Revolution, where he quickly distinguished himself in the Army of the North. His early career saw him serve under General Dumouriez and later under Napoleon during the Italian Campaign of 1796-1797, where his bravery and tactical skill earned him rapid promotions. He accompanied Napoleon to Egypt in 1798, participating in the Battle of the Pyramids and later commanding forces at the Battle of Heliopolis in 1800, before overseeing the French evacuation from Cairo in 1801. Upon returning to France, Belliard was named governor of Brussels and later participated in the Peninsular War, notably during the siege of Madrid in 1808 and its subsequent occupation, where he served as governor. His involvement in the disastrous Russian Campaign of 1812 saw him lead cavalry divisions, enduring the harrowing retreat. He continued to fight valiantly in the campaigns of 1813 and 1814, particularly at Leipzig and Hanau.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Belliard's career as a general under Napoleon, marked by participation in over 30 major battles and key administrative roles, significantly influenced the course of French military campaigns and occupations across Europe and North Africa. His ability to adapt to post-Napoleonic regimes further highlights the complex political landscape of early 19th-century Europe.
